To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed a simple and robust flow cytometry-based approach to quantify and characterize HIV-producing cells in the blood of people living with HIV, and that this approach revealed a broad diversity in phenotypes and activation states of HIV-infected reservoir cells in untreated and ART suppressed infection.
we developed a flow cytometry assay to quantify and phenotype HIV reservoir cells and applied it to untreated and treated HIV-infected individuals.
we developed and optimized an assay to quantify HIV-infected cells producing viral proteins in the blood of people living with HIV (PLWH).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new strategies to reduce the size of the HIV reservoir in order to cure HIV infection.
understanding and quantifying the HIV reservoir, which is the major barrier to HIV eradication.
the characterization of the cells and tissues in which the HIV virus persists in the human body, even after antiretrovial therapy (ART).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the p24 assay is an excellent and reliable method to quantify the number of productively infected T cells in HIV-infected individuals.

the HIV-1 infected cells that persist in ART-suppressed individuals are a heterogeneous population of cells, with some cells expressing activation markers and immune checkpoint receptors, but not others, and that the expression of integrin α4 is a common feature among these cells.

the HIV-1 reservoir is a heterogeneous mixture of different types of cells, which are not only different in their phenotype, but also in their transcriptional activity, and that this heterogeneity may be the main reason for the failure to eradicate HIV-1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a novel flow-cytometry based method to detect HIV-infected cells producing viral capsid in vivo.

we developed a simple assay to detect HIV-infected cells producing viral proteins in the blood of people living with HIV and that we characterized the phenotypes of these infected cells in both untreated and ART-supressed infection.
we have developed a simple and reliable assay to detect and quantify HIV-infected cells producing viral proteins in the blood of people living with HIV, both during untreated and treated infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a broad diversity in phenotypic characteristics among cells harboring the HIV reservoir in treated individuals.

the phenotypic characterization and quantification in blood of the cells that harbor replication competent virus during ART is now feasible and will be a powerful tool to better understand and characterize the HIV reservoir.

we have developed an assay that allows to quantify and phenotype HIV-infected cells from the blood of HIV-infected individuals, and that these infected cells are enriched in specific immune cells subsets.
